utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Good morning, everybody. Could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. All the accused are here. From the Defence teams I notice the absence of Mr. Haynes and Mr. Bourgon. I think that's about it. The Prosecution, Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Thayer. The witness Mr. Joseph is present. I take it there are no preliminaries, therefore we -- Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm simply rising to start my cross-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I was just going to ask you to precisely do that. Mr. Joseph --.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're still testifying pursuant to your solemn declaration of yesterday or of Friday [sic]. With some effort, we will ensure that we finish with your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse you had about 15 minutes more or something like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we begin this morning, Mr. Joseph, by looking at 6D30 which I hope is the agreement that you have made reference to in the course of your evidence. There it is. Might be worth looking at the top briefly to begin with. Agreement on disarmament of the military-able population in the enclave of Zepa. It says that today, 25th of July 1995, the following agreement was reached between Rajko Kusic on one side, Hamdija Kolak [phoen] from the other side, in the presence of Simon Dudnik as UNPROFOR representative. And it goes through the terms of this agreement. In particular, perhaps if we look at a specific part of it, have you ever seen the agreement before?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I might have seen it in the past, but I honestly, it's -- this is the first time I've seen it, if so, in a very long time, so it's not jumping out at me. I had been seen a draft agreement that David Harland and I had done that was a different draft demilitarisation agreement, but this does not prompt a memory in me immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you -- sorry, Mr. Josse, for interrupting you -- can you be specific as to Hamdija Kolak is, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's possible that meant Torlak instead of Kolak. That's all I can presume. Perhaps they meant Torlak and not Kolak.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's not for me to give evidence, Your Honour, but I think that that's a safe assumption to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked the question -- yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps my friend could also show the witness page 2, which also has another date on it, and just for the sake of making sure that he's had a chance to view the whole document before answering, it might be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I put my question because whoever that Hamdija Kolak, as it appears on the face of this document, is to have signed this, if he signed this, keep in mind -- you have to mind in mind that he is undertaking also on behalf of who was supposed to be the commander of the ABiH troops on the ground at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, indeed. The Court has already heard evidence as to that particular difficulty from this witness. I think the Court is going to hear more about that from General Smith in due course as well. Certainly the Defence are aware of that particular issue and/or difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that's why I asked who this Kolak is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If we do look at the second page, Mr. Joseph, first of all we see that it purports to be signed by Mr. Torlak among others and it also gives a different date, date of the 24th of July. We need to scroll down a bit in the English, please?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I might request, is it possible to just have a copy of this so I can read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You can have mine.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's not marked other than the fact I put the number on it. The usher will give it to you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm letting the witness read the document, Your Honour, although I in fact only have one supplementary question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When you are finished with reading it, Mr. Joseph, let us know, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It follows from what you've already said that this document was not being waved about by anyone presumably on the 26th of July when you returned to the enclave?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly don't recall it. If I can say a couple there's a couple other things to observe, if I may say so, number 1 being you just have the typed names here without signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's right. I'm not going to comment on that. The Court has heard some other evidence about this from other sources.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But dealing with my question, you don't recall people using the same expression, waving it around putting it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And in particular, the reference in paragraph 4 to weapons and equipment being returned and UNPROFOR members being unblocked?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No recollection of that, no, sir, and I might add in paragraph 5 it's rather unusual in an UNPROFOR, if UNPROFOR had a role in drafting this, that the weapons would be handed over to the BSA rather than to UNPROFOR. The standard is always weapons are submitted to the UN, not to an adversary or to a warring party.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As a matter of curiosity would be able to picture Mr. Dudnik?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I cannot. Don't remember that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Don't remember the name?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Don't remember the role he played?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't recall. I can't recall. If I had met him, I can't now 12 years later, I do not recall the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll be corrected if I'm wrong, I don't know whether it jogs your memory, he was the commander of the Ukrainian battalion?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One question sorry again, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of course. Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But this occurred to me when we heard, as you said, other evidence on this document. But at the time the opportunity to put the question had escaped me. If you look at the B/C/S version of this document, which you should have on your screen on your monitor now, paragraph 5, we see VBS there. VBS. Which -- is that a spelling mistake or what, VRS?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think I can shed some light on this. The B/C/S version is simply I believe an OTP or it may be a CLSS translation of this document. It's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of which document?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Of the English agreement that we were looking at a moment ago. So in other words, the B/C/S version is not a version that was created at the time. It is simply a translation of this English document, which we believe was created at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But my question was related to something somewhat different because the acronym BSA was in use amongst the UNPROFOR people and the other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, but I think that's a spelling mistake as Your Honour noted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the fact that on this English -- on the English version, the acronym BSA is used instead of VRS, is that -- would that be indicative that this was drawn up, that this was drawn up not by the Serbian side, but by UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, your question is that because they use BSA instead of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because a document originating from the VRS itself --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wouldn't use the acronym BSA in the first place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's quite possible. It's quite possible that that was the case, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Again, my apologies to you, Mr. Josse. You may proceed, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to move on. Could we have a look at 6D131? It's a completely different subject. Now, this is an article that we have found on the internet which purports to be written by you and was produced in the Washington Post on Sunday the 10th of July 2005 entitled "Bystander to a Massacre." Could I first confirm that you did in fact write an article that appeared in the Washington Post by that name at that time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it was written, wasn't it, in the aftermath of the discovery of the Skorpion video?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you express some background information about the video and about the events in Srebrenica, and initially on the first page, put it into context in relation to more modern day events, particularly in Darfur; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And with a specific reference, not to scale but to the fact that the presence I contrasted it with Darfur when there was then no -- probably still is no UN presence, but in Srebrenica there was UN presence. That's -- that was the reference, the contrast.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I am going to have to be for reasons of time constraint, selective, passages I want to ask you about. If you would go to the very bottom of this first page I'm going to read the final paragraph and then it will move over to the second page. "I have thought about these questions more than most. I served as a UN civil affairs officer in Bosnia for much of the three and a half years of war. My colleagues and I received the waves of women and children expelled from Srebrenica before their husbands, fathers, brothers and sons were executed. "About a week later, I found myself in Srebrenica, neighbouring enclave of Zepa, face to face with Mladic, an architect of the massacres. While his forces were finishing the slaughter in Srebrenica, he had turned his sights on Zepa's Muslim men. The Muslim commander, Colonel Avdo Palic, saved his soldiers by hiding them in the forest while he stayed behind to negotiate with Mladic. A colleague and I watched and protested vainly as Palic was seized by Serb troops from our collapsed UN compound and taken away and likely killed. "Because of this experience, and my feelings of responsibility towards Palic, I continue to ask why we let Srebrenica happen and why we don't act to prevent other tragedies. Over time I've come up with three answers." And it's right, isn't it, that you told us yesterday that you feel a sense of responsibility for what happened to Colonel Palic and you have tried to highlight his plight to the international community?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes that would be correct, and to assist his wife in getting the attention of the international community. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to pass over the first of your three answers. Basically you say that the United Nations needs staff who are less interested in money and more interested in doing a decent job but that's not of any relevance to this particular case. Second, even the vast majority who are motivated by the desire to do good may still find their principles compromised or confused by organisational loyalty. Many on the staff of the senior UN official in the former Yugoslavia, the Japanese diplomat, Yasushi Akashi, internalised his overarching priority to protect the UN's neutrality and even handedness by avoiding the use of force against the Serbs. Constantly -- beg your pardon, consistently, they rebuffed those who did advocate force like the UN's military commander in Bosnia, General Smith and toned down reports sent to New York to maintain the premise that all sides were equally guilty." Is that an objective approach?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe so. And if you would like to take the Court's time I would be happy to explain why I believe that's the case. In fact, I would suggest to save time, that if the Court or any of the parties here would refer themselves to the UN's own report on Srebrenica, you will see many of these points admitted to by the UN themselves, submitted by the then Secretary-General, Kofi Annan, who was earlier the head of DPKL and I think himself feels a good sense of responsibility. So you'll see many of these same points admitted to in a far more official way than my humble opinion piece here in the Washington Post.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: One other paragraph I'd like to look at. That's scrolling down, "The third and least understood factor in collective passivity toward evil is the prevalent taboo against, 'getting emotional' about death and tragedy. While there is always a risk of rushing to judgement or in allowing particularly graphic evidence to cloud decision-making, the greater risk is for exaggerated clinical detachment. Without a sense of guided outrage, of empathy for victims of abuse, organisation staff, even human rights workers, are prone to 'move on' and accept it when bureaucracies shrug their shoulders." Wasn't that the type of preconception that you had in mind when you went to Zepa on the 20ing of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. And it applied the same as it did to Serbs in Krajina or anyone else who was a vulnerable minority. So the attitude applies equally to anyone who is vulnerable, the point is that you do not simply shrug your shoulders, oh, let's be detached, let's be detached. And when you get too detached, then you forget that there is a question of human suffering involved. The question is whether you are equally concerned with suffering of Serbs, whether they be in Krajina or in Kosovo or in some other place, as you are with Muslims in this enclave or Croats in another location. That's the issue. Are you equally concerned about the plight of everyone as a human being and as an officer carrying out your duties? And as long as you are, then you're fulfilling your responsibility, but if you maintain a false premise of neutrality which is what the United Nations admitted in its report, a false obsession with neutrality as the overall guiding principle, and non-intervention in peacekeeping which then contorts the situation where you have to struggle in order to maintain your neutrality by suppressing and diminishing the reports that you have on one side and intensifying and exaggerating on the other. And I think that is the situation in Bosnia that was reported in quite some methodical detail by the United Nations in that seminal report on Srebrenica and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: These robust views of yours have clouded your judgement and recollection, I would suggest, of the events that you have described. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, that's your opinion, and I do not share that opinion, and I would say, add, to the extent that you imply as you do, that my memory is selective and that this is distorted and especially here as we have the accused listening, I will mention what a Bosnian Serb general told me at a meeting in airport in 1993. And he said to me, "You know, you come in here, it's like a fight, and you don't see when the first guy pushes and then you -- then we come back and hit someone, and then you come in and see and then you just see one side pushing." And what I tried to convey to you there were limits on what I understood and could witness in terms of Zepa. I arrived when arrived. I witnessed what I witnessed. And I reported to this Court what I remember. To the extent that it is -- does not for example, contain elements about attacks by Bosniak Armija on UNPROFOR, it's because I don't recall them, not because I don't wish to convey them. To the extent that they happened, I simply don't recall. I don't recall any Ukrainian officers complaining to me severely about that. In fact don't recall much of a role at all of the Ukrainian company there in this operation. We were doing most of the work and most of the guiding. They did some assistance, but it was our mission and I honestly don't recall that to the extent that that's what you're implying, so no I do not agree with you. And I try to remain true to my oath and report this as I recall it. That's all I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In conclusion, I'd like to put this to you: Do you agree with this proposition, that to navigate the thick waters of the Bosnian war is not so much an exercise in looking at deliberate dishonesty but of a contrived self deceit? This applies not only to many of the combatants but also to those who came with good intentions to try to make peace. In short, Mr. Joseph, I'm suggesting to you that you are guilty of self deceit. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What can I say? I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. That was translated for me. I've got nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have three other Defence counsel asking to cross-examine. There is Ms. Fauveau requesting one hour, Mr. Ostojic, 45 minutes and Mr. Zivanovic, 20 minutes. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, my name is Natasa Fauveau Ivanovic and I defend General Miletic. I would first like to ask you a few questions about Tuzla. The day before yesterday you said that the buses that had arrived with refugees to the base in Tuzla were not escorted by UNPROFOR; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, that is -- was the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Never, when those refugees were arriving from Srebrenica and Potocari, you were not at the dividing line between the Muslim and Serb forces, were you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is -- no, I was at the Tuzla air base.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know that the refugees were leaving -- were getting off Serb buses at the dividing line and then were getting on other buses that took them to their final destination, but these other buses had nothing to do with Serbs?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may be the case and it's possible that I knew that at the time at Kladanj. Kladanj was the normal crossing points so it's -- that part is true. I think perhaps what I -- to clarify what I meant was there was no UNPROFOR escort from Srebrenica or Potocari to Kladanj. The fact that they boarded UNPROFOR buses or some other buses, of course, no Serb driver could cross -- would or could cross that line from Kladanj and drive all the way to Tuzla. Of course, there would have to have been some transfer taking place at Kladanj. If I recall, that was the junction point.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But you were not in Kladanj, and do not know whether UNPROFOR vehicles had arrived with Serb buses to Kladanj or do you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not at Kladanj but as I understood the case, these were not UNPROFOR-assisted evacuation from Srebrenica. That was my understanding, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So you cannot say here under oath that you saw the buses arrive without Serb escort, in fact you know nothing about that, do you agree? I'm talking about the buses that came to Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And I wanted to add, without UN, without a UN escort. That came to Kladanj without a UN escort.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not witness to the arrival at Kladanj. That is correct. I was not witness there. I was under the understanding that I've already conveyed to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, if you don't mind, Ms. Fauveau. I accept that, as your explanation. However, did you, at any time, make it a point to receive or did you receive in any case reports from the escorts, UNPROFOR escorts or your escorts, as to the completion of the transportation of the civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, is your question -- did we get a notice that this is the last bus and no more buses are coming or something liking that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. What I mean to say is this: You obviously had a part to play in assigning escorts to accompany some of the buses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Me, personally?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, no, sir. I was at Tuzla air base assigned to receive -- assist, assist in the reception of these refugees who were coming in waves. We were at Tuzla air base. We were not at Kladanj. We had no role in terms of that movement from Kladanj to Tuzla, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who was in charge of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would imagine it would have been a military operation at Tuzla. There was Dutch control, there was a prominent Dutch role there. It was possible it was Dutch. It was also possible it was French because there was a French contingent in that Kladanj area. So it's quite possible it may have been French, sir, I'm sorry, I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, you have partly answered this question already, but do you know whether the UN or the UNHCR or any other international organisation such as the ICRC ever tried to go to Kladanj and escort the refugees from Kladanj to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There would have to have been UNPROFOR movement from Kladanj on. When I spoke earlier as I've said I was speaking about the movement from Srebrenica to Kladanj. There would have had to have been UN -- and very likely UNHCR, from Kladanj on. But Kladanj is essentially the same as Tuzla air base. It's already in an area that UN is active and operational in. We were not unfortunately - not because we didn't want to be - we were not permitted to be operational in Republika Srpska during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, I don't want an argument with you about this. But speaking about this concrete situation, you were in a position to go to the place where the Serbs forces left those refugees, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Me personally?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Not you personally. But UN staff.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course UN staff were in Kladanj. Of course. But this is already across the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke about an agreement, about the demilitarisation of Zepa that you proposed in the July 1995. That was on page 31 of yesterday's transcript. Isn't it correct that in July 1995, Zepa should have been demilitarised long ago?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. The original vision for all the safe areas was that they would be demilitarised. That's my recollection. That was the concept that they had.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And UNPROFOR and you personally, did you know in 1995 that Zepa was not demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have -- if there were fighting there, it -- again, Zepa was not my preoccupation until I was assigned to it. We may well have known. We may well have known. But it was not the exact number of arms or something like this, I don't know but we may well have known and even assumed that it was not demilitarised.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you say "we," who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean UNPROFOR and very likely I knew this, but again this was not the preoccupation of mine until I was moved and assigned, had this assignment, but that's correct. I believe it probably would be widely known in UNPROFOR that it was not demilitarised.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I understand that you personally were not preoccupied with that, but speaking generally about UNPROFOR in Bosnia, it was UNPROFOR's obligation to oversee the demilitarisation and to see to it that the demilitarisation is indeed carried out; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was correct. I'm drawing now on memory. I don't have the UN resolutions. There were a number beginning in 1993. There was a number of resolutions. I used to be able to quote some of them by heart, but as I recall, they were required demilitarisation and of course, they empowered the UN to call on NATO air strikes in a number of instances to "deter attacks," et cetera as far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And why was the demilitarisation of Zepa discussed only in July 1995 when it should have been demilitarised as early as May 1993?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a very fair and interesting question. I don't have the complete answer, but it would involve obviously some cooperation with the UN by both sides, and you would have to engage with others, perhaps General Smith and others, to find out where that cooperation was missing. As I said, we had very little access to Republika Srpska, including to these isolated enclaves. There was no civil affairs presence in Zepa at all ever, as far as I know. Very limited access to the other enclaves. There was that effort beginning in Srebrenica in 1993 started by General Morillon about demilitarisation and in exchange to have UNPROFOR protection, and others can speak far better than I to the details as to why those demilitarisation efforts came to -- had success or did not the have success and the relative responsibility of the parties much better than I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Have I understood you well to say that demilitarisation was not carried out or could not carried out because the Serbs didn't let you into those enclaves?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No [Interpretation] No, you have not understood me well. [In English] No. I'm saying that -- I am not the best witness to tell you exactly why these demilitarisation efforts did not come to pass. I'm suggesting to you that among the complicating factors was that we, UNPROFOR, only had -- we had very limited access in Republika Srpska anywhere, and so there might even be limitations as to even how much we know. But I can tell you surely that I'm not the best witness to explain to you why exactly the relative responsibility of the parties as to why these demilitarisation efforts did not achieve more success.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The demilitarisation proposal that you mentioned earlier, did you remember to whom you submitted that proposal in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We submitted as best I can recall, and I believe the documents show this, that we sent it on to our higher headquarters including to Zagreb, and we had informal discussions about it. I know one of the memos shows I discussed this with General Tolimir and quite possibly we might have had informal discussions on the Bosniak side as well about that. But formally, the document as the document was first submitted, up our chain of command in UNPROFOR as you wish.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show Exhibit number 5D413 to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, can you confirm that this is a memorandum from David Harland dated July 21st, 1995?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's certainly what it appears to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to go to page 2, the last paragraph. Sir, is this paragraph really about an informal conversation with General Tolimir during which you spoke to him about the proposals regarding demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably would have -- yeah, this is referring to a meeting where we would have raised this and discussed it and where he indicated his interest.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So it follows from this document that General Tolimir did not refuse that proposal?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But I don't know whether we actually showed him a copy and as you've seen from your copy of the document, the central provision of that demilitarisation proposal was that it had a role for NATO in terms of air strikes, and of course, we placed in it quite clearly that if the Bosniaks refused the agreement, or if they refused to comply fully in implementing the agreement, that that would be taken into account in calling NATO for air strikes. In other words that there would be an onus placed on both sides. That was our effort. That was what we were trying to do with this option, that was already there, under UN Security Council resolutions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would now like to show you document 5D416. This is also a UN document, a memorandum by David -- from David Harland. We see it is dated as 23 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Let us go to the second page of the document. Paragraph 2, please, on the screen. Sir, I'll give you some time to read this paragraph, which starts, "At about 2.00 p.m. this afternoon."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'hm. Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that according to this paragraph, you spoke at length with Mr. Bulajic and you spoke to him about that demilitarisation proposal also?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the record, yes, and I believe that to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And this Mr. Bulajic never opposed demilitarisation, at any case he didn't refuse it, or did he?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this memorandum, which I believe to be accurate, he did not. He -- he apparently showed some interest in and I believe that that's -- this is an accurate reflection of the record. That's -- that would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Mr. Bulajic was a representative of the civilian authorities of Republika Srpska, he was not a military person?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: About the situation in Zepa, and these talks, did you know who really ran these talks, who was -- who was -- who -- in charge of these talks? Were they military or civilian authorities, and please answer only if you really know the answer.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that -- with total certainty, that I know the answer. If that's the condition for me to answer, then I can't meet your condition.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Let us go back to your demilitarisation proposal. It seems based on the two documents that we've just seen, that the Serbs, both those from civilian structures as well as those from military structures, did not really oppose the demilitarisation proposal. Do you know why that proposal eventually was not realised?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ma'am, are you speaking about our demilitarisation proposal, the one of --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'll be happy to answer your question, and here I think I know the answer quite clearly. I can't say with total certainty, but I believe this to be the case. It never went anywhere because it included the express provision of NATO -- use of NATO air power, and I think for that reason, and 90 per cent that reason, it would have not been welcomed in the UN headquarters, and indeed, had it been presented formally to higher authorities in the Serb side in -- with that provision in it, I'm not so sure that the -- that might have been my acceptance. There might well have been interest in demilitarisation, but I'm not so sure that a start provision about calling in NATO air power would have been so welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You're speaking about the Serbs not accepting that possibly due to the NATO air strikes element but that is a speculation of yours. You never reached the final stage in these talks. So nobody ever clearly refused that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be correct. You could call it informed speculation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At any rate, UNPROFOR or the United Nations stopped that project regarding the demilitarisation. Do you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes. Again, I would refer you, if you have witnesses who are senior UNPROFOR military, it would probably be better to get the answer from them. It seemed to me very soon that we were beyond that, that there was a military situation that had quickly overtaken the situation that possibility of a demilitarisation agreement. At some point that was clear and that was again the role that we were called on to play which was to effect the evacuation of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to show you document 6D133, that you have already seen. It was yesterday. Yesterday, when you saw this document, you told us that it was possible that the person that the document is addressed to or the fighting that it is -- that is referred in this document might have been the fighting that you've already heard about. Is it possible that you told us that, that it was about the fighting that took place on the 20th of July 1995, and it is referred in this document? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm rereading your question to me. I didn't follow it. I'm just rereading here on the thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I believe that the interpretation did not come out very clear. The fighting that you spoke about yesterday, and that this document refers to, could this have been the fighting that you heard when you were in Zepa on the 20th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I believe I stated yesterday, yes. This could have been part of that fighting, could have been, absolutely could have been.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This is a document that originated from the Ukrainian force, and yesterday you spoke about some of the details of the document. However, when it comes to this particular document, do you have any doubt as regards the accuracy of the information that is conveyed in this document?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I see the entire document, please? It's simply stating that fighting began. So I can't be -- verify the exact time in there but the fact that fighting began, yes. The -- I can't speak to the -- necessarily as to whether the means used were simply those mentioned in this. This is a very short --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is two pages. You can see the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I didn't see the next page, sir. Thank you. Right. There is nothing there. This is -- if your question relates to -- does this document represent that there was fighting on that day and could this have been the initiation of what I heard, yes. Does it represent a full picture of what happened or was the fighting limited to the means mentioned, no, I can't speak to that, but it could well be that the fighting began that day and that that's what we heard part of.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Actually this document doesn't say only that the fighting had started. It, between the Republika Srpska army and the BiH army, with the use of certain means. I'm asking you this question because you also told us yesterday, at the beginning of your yesterday's testimony, that the source of fire that you heard was from the Serb positions, and in your testimony you never mentioned the BiH army at all. You only mentioned the Serb forces. Is that the case? Is it true that it is not just the fire coming from the positions of the Republika Srpska army but that it was actually a battle going on between the two sides?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ma'am, I would repeat what I said earlier about the conversation way back and what the Serb general said. You only saw part. I can only testify as to those events that I saw and witnessed. I'm sorry if I can't testify as to the activities of the Armija. I cannot. I cannot say that what they were doing or what they weren't doing. I can only tell you the part that I saw. I was only at OP 2. That was Serb-controlled. That's the only part that I can testify to. I think you can find other witnesses who can give far better testimony than I can as to what the Armija was doing. I concede it's quite possible that they were engaged in a fire-fight. I simply, as this witness, cannot testify to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, when you were there, how could you determine that the source of fire came from the Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- it -- the -- it's quite possible even that we saw firing. You're asking me about events that were 12 years ago. But it is quite possible we saw positions, gunnery positions, and it was clear to us that the spot where we were, this high ground, was completely controlled by the Serb military. That to us was clear. There were various weapons and vehicles associated with that. It would be hard for me now 12 years later to identify, but it was quite clear to me that this was under control and that there were significant presence of weapons. And the firing we heard was from this side. It sounded to us from the way we gauge it; although, hearing is notoriously misleading for anyone. Hearing is not a good indicator but for us, it certainly appeared that this was outgoing. And we didn't see any indication from the Serbs of indication of incoming, such as soldiers running for cover or telling us to take shelter or we didn't see that, we didn't see any indication of what one would expect from a disciplined unit, as the Serbs -- Serb army was, of taking incoming fire at the location where we were.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, didn't you say that actually at the given moment, the situation became rather tense and that the Serbs actually told you that you were better off leaving the area?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't tell us we were better off to leave. They told us to leave. Now, if you want to -- it's fair, if you want to say that they did it out of concern for our safety, you can have that inference. I'm telling you I can only testify as to what I observed. At the time there was a quite serious demeanour. I did not see running for shelter. I saw the appearance of military activity. And we were told to leave. That's what I witnessed. That's what I've testified to.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to show you Exhibit 6D91. Yesterday you saw the document. I did not intend to show it to you but I will do nevertheless. Does this document originate from the observation point at which you were located?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document itself, one cannot say where the precise location of the document. It isn't necessarily that this was the same specific location. This may well have been. It says targeted the barracks of Ukrainian company. That could have been down and more likely was down in Zepa town, not where we were at the OP 2 in all likelihood, in all likelihood.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: According to you, the Bosnian force, the Armija, shelled the city of Zepa, and I suppose that it was inhabited by civilian population, that it was only civilian population that was there when the army shelled it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am -- the paragraph Charlie that I'm reading says three mortar rounds directly targeted the barracks of Ukrainian company, numerous explosions registered, also has been hit with a small arms and heavy machine-gun, origin of fire is Armija of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's correct. That's what they are reporting. This witness cannot testify one way or the other as to this, as -- because this witness wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to move on to another topic. I would like to show you Exhibit numbers 5D417. Sir, you have already had an opportunity to see this document. You saw it yesterday. And you were asked about it by my learned friend just a while ago. I would like to show you paragraph 3, which is towards the end of this page. Do you remember that you actually saw this document yesterday and that you discussed it with my learned friend?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that is correct, yes. We looked at this document yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember that yesterday you told us that at the time, which means -- yesterday you told us that -- or actually the day before yesterday, you told us that you saw a copy of the document or the document that this document makes reference to?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not really following you. Are you asking do I recall actually seeing this document at the time? Is that your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: No. Sir, no, I'm not asking you this. I'm simply asking you to confirm whether you remember that you told us yesterday that you believe that you had seen this document before, when I'm talking about the document I'm talking about the agreement.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's what I said yesterday, I stand by that. I don't have a vivid present recollection of this document, if that's your question. I do not. This -- these reports strike me as accurate and plausible and it's indeed quite likely that I saw this document at the time. But it was Viktor who is reported to have called it in, so it's possible that he was actually holding the document or something or, you know, had more closer scrutiny of it than I did at the time. It's possible as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And if you could look at the last paragraph, under 6, it mentions the agreement and based on that agreement the civilian population of Zepa was supposed to be provided with an opportunity to declare themselves as to where they wished to reside from then on. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's certainly what this says, and I have no reason to believe that that was not in the document at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you arrived in Zepa, during the evacuation campaign, you actually started inquiring among the people whether they wanted to leave or, rather, whether they wanted to stay; is that correct? This is a very simple question, sir.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This agreement was something that provided for the Muslim forces surrendering. This is what is stated under 2 and 4, Muslim forces were supposed to surrender, according to this agreement.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among other things, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true, maybe you didn't know it at the time, but I believe that you know it now, that the government in Sarajevo did not want to ratify this agreement, that they would not accept it as such?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible. I'm not sure what I knew about that but that's quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we show page 2 of this document to the witness, please? Can we go to the paragraph which begins with the following words, "At 11.40 a.m.". According to this document, Minister Muratovic says that he did not know anything about this document, about this?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question is?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you confirm that according to this paragraph, Minister Muratovic did not know anything about the agreement or at least that is what he said?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's clearly what it says. I have no other basis of knowledge. I can't shed any more light on it but that's clearly what it says, and I have no reason to doubt the accuracy of this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: If you look at the last paragraph of this document, Minister Muratovic expressed a certain doubt about the existence of Hamdija Torlak, he doubted whether Hamdija Torlak actually existed?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But you yourself knew that Hamdija Torlak did exist?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew that he existed but I didn't know his exact position or function or his competence to effect or not effect agreements. But that is correct, I knew that he existed, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What we can also see in this document, which is the penultimate paragraph, is that the Bosnian government was not at all contrary to the evacuation of the Muslim population from Zepa. They did not oppose it at all. Actually, what they wanted was for the evacuation to be carried out under certain conditions.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is your question, please, ma'am? I'm sorry, I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, is it true that the paragraph starting with at 11.40,"I called minister Muratovic," and so on and so forth, confirms that the government in Sarajevo was not opposed to the evacuation of the population from Bosnia -- from Zepa as long as it was carried out under certain conditions and the conditions were those that the UNPROFOR supervised the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What my -- I can give you my best judgement on this. I wouldn't -- I wouldn't make a complete inference as to the total position of the Bosnian government from this paragraph. It depends very much on the context, and I'm not here to speak on behalf of the Bosnian government and you should -- those officials are still alive and can speak for themselves and represent what it was -- what their position is. It seems to me the paragraph stands on its face. The minister is expressing concerns with respect to what happened in Srebrenica. Beyond that, how much you want to infer is up to you. It's not really for me to state.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In any case, finally, when the evacuation was finished, it was actually carried out in the full presence of the UNPROFOR. The UNPROFOR was there all the time.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And it was also carried out before the Muslim forces in Zepa surrendered?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be correct to say that what happened in Zepa, was the evacuation of the Zepa population, was not the success of Mladic but the success of the government in Sarajevo. Actually it was not Mladic who succeeded by evacuating the population from Zepa. It was the government of Sarajevo and the Muslim forces who succeeded because the Muslim force remained armed after the evacuation of the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ma'am, is it my role here to ratify your judgements and inferences? I just don't understand -- I'm not sure that this is my role here as a witness. I understood that I was called to this Tribunal to testify as to the events, the observations. If you're asking me for opinions, I'm happy to give them about the total context of this. I'm happy to share those. It would be as an expert and not as a fact witness. But I'm not sure that this is really my role.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Fauveau and Mr. Joseph. You haven't been summoned here as a witness -- as an expert witness. You've been summoned here as a witness to the facts that you are -- that are to-- that you are aware of. So please, we are not interested, and I'm using this language not in any disparaging way, we are not interested in your opinions because you haven't been called here to express opinions. So if you think that by answering Madam Fauveau's question you would be making an assessment, giving an opinion, which you wouldn't like to give, then you only have to ask not to answer the question. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That having been say, of course, Madam Fauveau, you can rephrase, reformulate your question, without asking the witness to give an expert opinion. I could also add that the gist of your previous question to him has more of the nature of a submission than anything else, but I don't want to stop you from reformulating your question or putting a different one.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that Minister Muratovic said that once the evacuation was finished, before the evacuation was completed, the evacuation of the civilian population was complete, the Muslim forces of Zepa would not surrender, they would not surrender their weapons?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- it says what it says. The document says what it says. I'm sorry, I've lot track of the document. I'm not trying to be difficult. There is nothing more I can add to this. The document speaks for itself. I've attested that I believe it to be an accurate record.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how I can better answer the question. Minister Muratovic's position is reflected, I believe to be accurately reflected, in this document and it stands on its own. I don't know that I can shed any more light on this than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, my question was not related to this document. I wanted to show you another one, but for the time being I'm asking you this. Did you know that Minister Muratovic stated, once the evacuation was completed, that the Muslim forces of Zepa would not surrender? If you don't know, you can simply say, "I don't know about that."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may know this if we stop and look at the record but sounds to me a plausible position that you make, as to his position, but I'm not -- here I'd have to refer back to some more documents to confirm that but that sounds like a plausible position.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness Exhibit number 5D419. Sir, this is a document dated 27 July. This is a memorandum originating from David Harland.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Please understand me. I'm asking you this because the accused don't have a copy of this document in the language that they understand. That's why some of my questions seem pretty straightforward. This is just to help them understand what the document is about. In the second paragraph of this document, a reference is made to a telephone conversation that you had and during which you said, at -- that at 2.00, a majority of the civilian population had already been evacuated.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we now show the witness page 2 of the same document? In the penultimate paragraph, we are talking about 5.00 in the afternoon of the same day, Minister Muratovic called and said that the Bosnian military in the pocket would not surrender.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, would it be the convenient time for our first break? And after the break, I will require another ten to 15 minutes approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Yes, certainly, Madam Fauveau. Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President I don't want to pre-empt Your Honour, but if we could have an estimate from my friends about how much time they have left, you typically do this, but I just wanted to emphasise we have -- our next witness is an investigator who is multi-tasking all the time, and we just want to be able to manage his time as best as possible, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I have it for the time being it's another 15 minutes from Madam Fauveau. Mr. Ostojic, do you still require 45 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. I'll re-evaluate. I think about a half hour to 45 minutes. It's hard to gauge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: For the time being I stay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we are where we stood before. 45 minutes to be on the safe side, plus 20, that's an hour and five minutes, plus 15, an hour and 20 minutes. Basically we should finish if there is re-examination, we should finish by the end of the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you continue, Ms. Fauveau, for the record Judge Stole had to leave us, unfortunately, and we are proceeding with the sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Yes. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement, you spoke much about the evacuation from Zepa. Can we say that the role you played in that evacuation, both personally and as a member of an international organisation, was an active one?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And, in effect, you and your colleague, Viktor Bezruchenko, as well as local Muslim leaders, organised the -- for the civilian Muslim population to board buses?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We weren't solely organising. We organised one part of it and coordinated part of it, but it isn't as though we organised ourselves, everything, but you're correct that the Bosniak or Muslim leaders had their role and we had our role and the Serbs had their role.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please show the witness Exhibit number 4D111.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This is a statement about the telephone conversation which you had in April 2005, with a representative of the OTP. Could we see the third page, please? I'm referring to paragraph 14. Sir, I'm going to read out this -- what this report says. This is a report about the interview with you, and I will ask you whether you adhere to what you said then. "We started to organise the civilians boarding in the vehicles. I, Viktor, and at least one French officer were very active on this as well as some of the Muslim leaders. I can recall seeing also General Smith there observing the evacuation."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a very accurate rendering of what I said to this reporter. It's not completely accurate. General Smith was not there that I recall, "Observing" the evacuation. I couldn't rule it out categorically. But it isn't -- that part of it seems -- it's not a complete -- completely accurate picture. We were there. We did start to organise, Viktor and I were there. At one point during the evacuation, yes, there was one French officer who -- who we were cooperating with. That's right. But I can't say that this paragraph is a completely accurate rendering either of what I said to him or what I observed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to focus on what is said about General Smith. You say that you don't remember seeing General Smith observing the evacuation. But you cannot rule that out categorically. Does that mean that today you no longer remember whether General Smith actually observed the evacuation process?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that I don't believe this is either an accurate reflection of what I said, even to this reporter, or accurate as to what I observed at the time. What I recall vividly was being at a meeting with General Smith and Colonel Baxter at the top, at OP 2. I don't recall General Smith observing the evacuation. The fact that I don't recall it doesn't mean categorically that it didn't happen. I might not have seen him at some point. I'm just saying when I made this statement, and now, that that part of it is not right, and I don't believe I even made that statement to the person who reported -- I think the person misunderstood. It was done over the telephone. The person who did it was a non-native English speaker, and it's quite possible there was some misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: De rien.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, you are mentioning a French soldier. I'm no longer referring to the statement. I'm asking you about the events at that time in Zepa. Is it correct that UNPROFOR, during that evacuation, deployed additional forces?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And a little while ago, you spoke about these international forces arriving at Zepa without any problems, although you had been saying that reaching the enclave was problem -- was a problem, or I'm going to repeat the question. Recently, you spoke about the difficulties that the international organisations had reaching the enclave generally speaking, in the general sense. But these UNPROFOR forces that had arrived to assist in the evacuation were able to reach Zepa without problems?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes, absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that while you were actively involved in that evacuation, and while you were in Zepa, that you received no orders from General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a member of the United Nations, I cannot receive then -- cannot receive orders from any military or political official who is not in the United Nations so that's an impossibility. Did -- did General Mladic instruct us -- this is when you will go down and then did we comply? And yes we went down, or this is the way we are going to do the things? Yes. But formally speaking, I can't take orders from any general, nor political leader, of any side in a party of that conflict. But instructions as to how to -- the modalities for this, were there -- was direction given? Yes, direction was given.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you agree that under no circumstances General Mladic could give even instructions to General Smith?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He couldn't instruct, but he could convey his views as to how something would go, the same as any military leader of any faction, Bosniak or Croat, but that is a true statement. General Smith can only be ordered within his chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In any case, General Smith would never have followed any suggestion or instruction from General Mladic that would result in infringements of international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would tell you this: I have the highest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we have reached the limits of this line of questioning with respect to what General Smith would or wouldn't do. He will be here as a fact witness about the events in Zepa. The witness has already testified about whether he could take orders from General Mladic, but I think that's sufficient for this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I stand to be directed by my colleagues, but I think this is a question that should be directed to General Smith and he is best-placed to answer it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, if General Mladic had given you an instruction that would be contrary to international humanitarian law, you wouldn't have followed that instruction; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not -- my -- as I told you, we were, for example, told under international humanitarian law you have to determine the volition of the person to depart, and I told you and explained to this Court what happened and how to disregard it. So I can't say strictly we had in our mind the safety and security, as best we could preserve the dignity, but really it was primarily the safety and security of the people who were being evacuated. Whether that conformed 100 per cent with international humanitarian law, whether that was even in our mind at every point, I can't say. What was in our mind at every point was the safety and security of the evacuation. That is it. And we would weigh of course what General Mladic would or would not say at -- and weigh that. If it would have imperiled the safety and security. If he had directed us to do something that I felt, speaking for myself, would have imperiled these people in some way, within the confines of the peril they were already in, no, I wouldn't have followed that. I don't know if I've answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You have answered my question completely. And I will go a little further now. Is it correct that in wartime situations, in situations of serious crises, when the -- the conflicting parties are sometimes forced to take certain steps to protect civilian population and these steps being on the verge of a legal standards and provisions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, if you think that this is a question that you shouldn't answer because it belongs to an expert witness, you're free to ask us not to answer it. Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I explain, Your Honour? The witness repeatedly stated that he has rather great experience, he even said unique experience, in the context of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia. That's why I asked this question. But if he thinks that this is not an appropriate question, I shall withdraw it, in fact I wanted to say if the Chamber thinks that this question shouldn't be answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think if you wish to ask such questions, I mean, you need to phrase them in a way such as not to elicit an opinion, but to seek what his own personal position was at the time. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I misunderstood. I thought I was awaiting for the respected, esteemed attorney, to rephrase the question. I thought that was what you were getting at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: More or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm waiting for your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I will continue and perhaps a little later on I will ask a similar question. So what I'm about to ask you now has nothing to do with my previous question. Yesterday, on page 37 of the transcript, you said that Serb soldiers had a full liberty in the area of the other enclave which was in fact under the control of Ukrainian soldiers. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But Avdo Palic, who was the commander of the Muslim forces in that enclave, also had a full liberty of movement?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had full movement in the area of the village. I don't think he had full movement towards the area towards OP 2. Where I saw his -- witnessed his movements free and unconstrained were in the village, and then back up toward the hills wherever he was going and wherever the men were hidden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Sorry, Madam Fauveau, and you are basing this assessment on what you could see at the time that you were there and not on other information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Exclusively saying what I could observe with my own eyes was Colonel Palic could move about, as we were moving about, in the village at the time of the evacuation, and in the evenings, some points when he decided during the day he would go up into these hills behind us. I don't recall him walking freely up towards OP 2, towards that initial position where we were, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I meant to say is that you couldn't account for his movements or the extent to which he could move around in the area at a time when you were not present.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be correct. I can only relate what I observed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: During the evacuation, and the boarding of the population in buses and vehicles, you never saw anybody being forced to board a vehicle or bus?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If you mean physically, with someone pointing a gun, no. I've already related to you, I believe, to this Court, the fact that it was clear that the issue of volition was already well passed and that these people felt themselves under duress. That was their reason for their departure.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you asked the inhabitants whether they wanted to leave, nobody prevented you from asking them that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you put that question to some 15 or 20 persons, didn't you, and only one person said that he or she wanted to say but was -- stay, sorry, but was afraid?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Going on my recollection, that is correct. Only one person said that she didn't want to go, and all of them cried. One said no; all of them cried with her. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When that person said to you she was afraid, and when you doubted her will to leave, did you inform your superiors of that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am. And not that I recall that we even had means but the answer to that is no, did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you inform General Smith about that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you inform General Mladic or even General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when you arrived in Zepa or on the next day, you saw that group of people in the centre of Zepa. You didn't expect to see them there, did you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not sure really what to expect, and we were sort of surprised. We anticipated that we would have to go and sort of group the people, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And in your statement, you spoke on several times about impressions. When you saw that large group of people in the centre of Zepa, did you have the impression that those people wanted to leave?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking for my impressions, and I'm happy to share my impressions with you. My impressions were those people, let's see, your question, wanted to leave. My impression is that these people were afraid for their lives. That's my impression. When someone is afraid for their lives, they want to leave. That's my impression.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You personally also, with regard to your experience in the war in former Yugoslavia, you went to several places where there were conflicts, and you had seen crises in other parts of the world too. Can we say, speaking about the people in Zepa, that the fear they felt was more caused by the general situation and the general tension between the ethnic groups after the years of war rather than that -- rather than being due to the situation on that day in Zepa itself?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked this based on my experience, and I can relate this to other areas of former Yugoslavia where I was, and I would say the answer is it was -- the fear was related in my view, in my impression, to this specific situation of being overrun, and I can compare it, if you wish, you mentioned my experience, there was an evacuation of Croats that I participated in in January 1993 following a Croatian attack at Maslenica Bridge. Then a number of Serb forces and Serb irregulars, including Arkan and Captain Dragan came into Krajina, and a number of Croat civilians were killed. And these Croats had been living in, as minorities in Krajina, among the Serbs. They had been living. And it was this change to the situation that injected a situation of crisis, that where some of them had been killed in Drnis and other places, some old people had their throats slit. And that created this atmosphere of great fear and panic. So where they had actually been living under Serb control for sometime, all of a sudden they were afraid and wanted to leave. I would compare it to that situation and say that there had been a change. That these people seemed to be terrified by this change in the situation and that that was their immediate desire to leave. Can I exclude the possibility that they had been isolated and deprived for sometime and that some of them might have wanted to go? I cannot exclude that possibility, but to me drawing on my experience, you're asking for my -- based on my impression based, on my experience, I'm sharing that with you, it was the latter. It was the change situation, an immediate crisis in which these people felt immediately in fearful of their lives, that's my impression.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In this particular case of Zepa, fear was caused by the entry of the Serbs in Zepa, the taking of Zepa, which was a consequence of the military victory of the Serbian army; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And that couldn't be avoided, could it? What I'm -- what I want to say is, if a military operation is -- takes place, and one side wins, then the defeated side is scared. I'm referring to this concrete moment in July 1995. In 1992 it may have been different, but could anything else be done for the people to avoid the people being scared?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer? Before you answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've risen to object initially because the question really was asking, sounded like for speculation, then it got concrete again it seemed. But then it in, my opinion, reverted to again asking a very generalised speculative question. If he feels like he has the -- as Your Honour has made clear before, he has the factual basis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think -- I read the question and again - I stand to be corrected by my colleagues - but I read the question to be Mr. Joseph, having given us an expose on the events in Krajina in 1993 and having lived through the events in Zepa in July 1995, isn't that -- isn't it true that there was a difference in the circumstances? And this is what the question amounts to, and I think he can answer it. Okay. So that's the gist of the question. If it's not the gist of the question, as I understood it to be, then please tell me, Madam Fauveau, but I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is somewhat different. What I'm interested in is the following:

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At that moment in Zepa, after three or four years of war, was there anything to prevent the people from being scared, after there had been a military victory of one of the warring parties? Could anything be done to prevent the population from -- of the other warring party from being scared? And I said maybe at the beginning of the war, it was possible, that is in 1992, it was possible, maybe, to find a different solutions.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to wait. Let me try to read your question here specifically on the screen. "Could anything be done to prevent the population from being scared?" Of course, theoretically many things could be done to redress the fear of a population. You might think first among them a deployment of UNPROFOR. Well, their confidence in UNPROFOR I think would have been rather low, if not non-existent at that point, and the ability to deploy an adequate detachment especially coming right after the fall of Srebrenica and the situation of the Dutch troops there, I think that was not a possibility. One can think of other things that could be done. There is a panoply of things that could be done to restore confidence. Some --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or something else, some agreement, a political agreement, a peace agreement. Many, many things that could be done. I'm still struggling my best to answer your question. I'm just not sure, maybe I don't understand the thrust of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I believe that you have understood my question very well and you have answered it, as a matter of fact. You said that most natural thing was to deploy the United Nations, but there were United Nations forces deployed when the Serbs entered the village; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's exactly correct. And that's the point. They were completely ineffectual and we should also point out that this comes contemporaneous with the fall of Srebrenica which no doubt this population was aware of and quite possibly was aware of some of the events following the fall of Srebrenica.
