So it's quite possible that this influenced their mental state and their attitude of great fear.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You have also mentioned the signing of an agreement, and it seems that there was an agreement that was co-signed by the Ukrainian Battalion of the United Nations protection forces.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I point out before, I was shown that agreement. I don't recall seeing that agreement. Mr. Josse kindly showed me that agreement. But as I pointed out then, I don't recall actually seeing signatures to it, so I don't know that it was -- it was possibly a draft. You'll notice that the one David Harland and I had was sort of equal stature. It was an unsigned draft. I can't exclude the possibility that a signed copy exists. The copy I was shown was unsigned. That's the only thing I point out but Mr. Josse did indeed show us that copy and I did see it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In any case, this was a very particular situation in Zepa, and the evacuation of the civilian population was a situation in which the Serbs showed the willingness to eventually allow people to remain in Zepa, if they so wanted.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't exclude that possibility. I can't exclude that possibility. Perhaps, if someone had wanted to remain, I can't exclude that possibility, that that -- that would be true. I know that the -- our understanding was clear, that our mission was to evacuate, Serbs provided the vehicles, and we assisted and helped coordinate this onward movement. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Fauveau. Who is going next, Mr. Ostojic or Mr. Zivanovic? Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Joseph. As you know, my name is John Ostojic and I represent Mr. Ljubisa Beara. How are you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm fine, good morning to you. [Interpretation] I give my regards to everybody present.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a couple of questions today, and I hope not to be repetitive. I'd like first to have a better understanding of your position as a civil affairs officer. Was your immediate boss and supervisor the senior civil affairs officer, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he explained yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- who his superior was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir we looked at some of these memorandums or situation reports that you outlined for us. In some of them your name appears directly under Mr. Harland's and in others it does not. Can you explain to me why in some of them your name appears on it and in others it doesn't?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think on the ones that would appear, David would have been trying to show that this was a collaborative effort probably that's -- that would be the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As a civil affairs officer, in 1995, were you required to maintain records and notes while negotiations were on going between various warring or political parties?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No requirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How would you be able to convey any of the demands of one party, if you met, as you've testified already, with Minister Muratovic, how would you be able to recall and convey that information to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whoever would be senior in that meeting would convey and normally would be fastidious with a record. Whether there was a written requirement to do that would be something else, but normally would be fastidious with notes but the senior person would convey that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When were you tasked to go to Zepa in July of 1995, were you given written instructions as to what your task was?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your task, and I think your job at that point, was to attempt to evacuate the civilians of Zepa, correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my understanding of what our role was to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just briefly, although I think you can explain it and you may have already, the purpose to evacuate the civilians because there was a war going on and there was fighting and the use of, as you describe before, both small and very heavy machine-guns and mortars and other types of ammunitions, correct? And to get them out of harms way in essence, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. That would not be an accurate. It was because of a specific situation where this enclave, like the one before it, Srebrenica, had fallen. That is the -- was the specific triggering event for this evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned just briefly on page 44 just moments ago that there was a loss of confidence in UNPROFOR, although you surmised that by the people in Zepa and then you said that it was not possible to deploy a detachment of UNPROFOR. What would a reasonable detachment be to send out to Zepa in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reasonable size?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would refer you more to reports of the UN Security Council which they prepared their own three options light, medium, and heavy. I'm sure it's well known to the Court and others. It's probably more authoritative than what I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, would you consider 150 UNPROFOR troops to be, if that's a figure that I'd use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could have some specificity as to when in July of 1995 we are talking about, because that could make a tremendous difference if we are really talking about what options were available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sir, I think that's a fair comment. At the same time, I think you are also moving a little bit too fast. Please allow a short pause between question and answer. You both speak the same language and it's creating a little bit of difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know you will, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm just drawing your attention because you've been overlapping actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't agree with my learned colleague's objection. I don't know if the witness, if it makes a difference for the witness, but for the sake of going on how about if we just pick the date of the 26th of July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. And let's stick to that, then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you would be good enough to restate the question, sir, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's take the 26th of July 1995. What would you consider the deployment of 150 UNPROFOR troops coming into the enclave of Zepa [indiscernible], immediate, light or large?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you, the question of the size of that contingent is in my view relevant but secondary to the willingness to use all aspects of the safe area resolution, including NATO air power. That was where the real deterrent lied, especially at that point after the situation in Srebrenica with the overrunning of the Dutch troops. So the actual size, others are far more expert than I in determining precisely the number of troops needed from a ground perspective. From my perspective that was secondary to the willingness and ability to use NATO air power. What would have provided confidence to the people on the ground is -- would be difficult to say how much.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. As a fact witness, Mr. Joseph, are you aware that in on or about July 25th and 26th, 1995, actually there is a deployment of about 150 UNPROFOR troops to the Zepa enclave?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be correct as a part of the evacuation. Their mission is not to stay, and as I reported as soon as the wounded convoy left, this was -- triggered great panic among the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So would I be wrong sir to suggest to you that the deployment of those 150 UNPROFOR troops was for the reinforcement of the Ukrainians that were there? Would that be incorrect?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say respectfully that would be incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's look at 6D29, as it's coming up, you were telling us a little bit about Lieutenant Colonel Baxter. Would you refresh my recollection how he fits into the hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think his title was military assistant to General Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And this is 6D29 is a sit report, a situation report, captioned memorandum from David Harland with the initials "SCVAO," which is just Senior Civil Affairs Officer, correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now just quickly Directing your -- and you saw this report yesterday, directing your attention to the last page and the second paragraph of that page. I'll give you a chance to read it, but my first question is this is a report being written by Harland, so it seems as if Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter is giving him this information, correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Just read the second paragraph, really, the first sentence is what we are discussing now.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is -- I read it and yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, in that, doesn't it clearly say that Baxter reported that UNPROFOR had deployed about 150 additional troops into the enclave to reinforce the 79 Ukrainians there?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does, it does -- it does. It doesn't say to reinforce them in what mission. It doesn't say. And I would -- my recollection is their mission was not to remain in place and secure as permanent deployment in the safe area. That's my impression, military obviously, General Smith and others can state it far more authoritative than I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We will ask them, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, also we discussed briefly, and you saw in the video yesterday, I think, the ICRC truck; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And now do you remember that on or about July 26th, 1995, there were actually two ICRC teams in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I recall and what I testified to is that I recall ICRC being there exclusively to deal with the evacuation of the wounded, and it would have been on that day, probably that was the day, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would you remember if there was more than one team?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I can't be sure of.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Help me understand this: How many people constitute an ICRC team?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not for me to say. I have to defer you respectfully to ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just look at the next sentence in that same Exhibit 6D29. There senior civil affairs officer David Harland seems to say in addition to UNPROFOR civil affairs, a JO team and two ICRC teams were in the pocket. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And sorry, I'm being told that I'm overlapping with you and I apologise. It's making it difficult for everyone, so I'll try to be more patient?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe it would be easier in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to speak Serbian with you because it would make me look bad. [In English] I don't know if that was a correct translation. I think he can verify it but okay. Sir, is there any reason to dispute that which we see on Exhibit 6D29, which is a memorandum from David Harland to John Ryan?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't dispute what you see there. If it's the reference to two ICRC teams, no, but whether a team constituted two vehicles or not, I simply can't recall that detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I understand that, and we'll have some other people who can perhaps help us out with that. I'd like to ask you a little bit about that which you mentioned on page 48 yesterday, line 12, and that was a book that you seem to have with you while you were in Zepa in 1995 called "The Documents on the Laws of War." Do you remember that, mentioning that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And who is the author of that book?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- there is -- it's an edited legal treatise. It contains the Geneva Conventions and assorted other things. I don't know what the -- if there is an author or someone who compiled it, I don't know who it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who issued the book to you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my own book.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So you brought that from America when you went on your first mission?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And did you carry it with you when you went to Africa as well?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not on a conflict mission in Africa, but I had it with me in every conflict place in former Yugoslavia, and I believe I took it to -- with me to Iraq in 2004 when I was in Iraq.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And do you still have that book?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And who else other than yourself had that book in the former Yugoslavia in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Former Yugoslavia is a big country. I don't know who else would have had that book.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If you had -- if you know, did David Harland would have it or John Ryan, would they have had a copy of that book as well?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but they might have had copies of the Geneva Conventions and other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, sir, the honourable Judge Prost asked you a question, and I believe it was on line 12, I mean page 12, lines 9 through 11, and she asked you, and this is while you were still in Tuzla, what kind of information did you have on the status of the Bosnian Muslims at that time. Do you remember generally the question?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, if it's a question I'm recalling, the Honourable Judge Prost asked me about the information we had about the men of Srebrenica, if I'm recalling the right question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That is correct. I think you answered, sir, without specifically citing it, that you had talked to or heard from General Smith that he talked to General Mladic, et cetera. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. I believe I stated that a senior -- I asked a senior UNPROFOR officer what had happened to the men, and I was told I was relayed as I recall, that General Mladic had said --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Men were released?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Men were released, some of them were released and that they are making their way back, they're walking there. That's what I recall being told. Sir, just a point of reference on that -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you try on the 19th of July 1995, while you were in Tuzla, to obtain any information from the ABiH about the Muslim men in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. And no, and not that I would believe that they would have any information. We were consumed with dealing with the refugee influx, and getting our own people out. There was an interpreter, civilian, Bosniak interpreter, who we were in telephone contact with in Srebrenica and he, I can remember speaking to him on the line directly, he was terrified because the Dutch were going to pull out and leave him behind, and he was desperate and asked for our assistance, and we provided it. And I got an instruction to the Dutch that said basically you will not leave without getting this guy out.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, I'm not sure I understand your answer fully, so if you can help me. Why is it that you think the ABiH wouldn't have information about his own military men who were coming through a forest or in a column?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, they were not my, as a civil affairs officer, primary interlocutor. At that time, our mission as civil affairs was focused on dealing with this civil influx, the refugee influx. That's first. Second answer, if you want me to give a larger answer, I don't know what kind of means captured military men would have to convey back to their headquarters about their situation. Perhaps I don't know, maybe I'm missing something.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure how the word "captured" got into the equation. Let me show an exhibit in a moment, but it's our information sir that the United Nations knew, as early as July 19, 1995, that at least 4.000 ABiH men who were coming through this column made it to Tuzla and most of them were soldiers, some of them were civilians. Do you remember seeing any of that influx of men who were soldiers of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was at Tuzla air base, and I don't recall hearing of this or seeing it. I cannot recall that. At the time that I was at Tuzla air base, nor do I remember hearing of it when I was returned to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me show you 2D17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just ask my friend to disclose the list of documents they intend to use on cross-examination. We haven't received it yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: All the documents are in e-court, and we didn't anticipate using this document until we heard the testimony, and I don't think there is any others -- that's not the right one, actually -- but I can give him a hard copy with some of my notes on it if the Court is willing and counsel to accept that, but I have it down as 2D17 which is previously identified and marked as an exhibit; which is the report, if I can just identify for the record, dated the 19th of July 1995 to Mr. Annan at the United Nations New York from Akashi, UNPF-HQ, Zagreb with the initials following. The report we've seen previously with Mr. Ruez among other witnesses, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you satisfied with that explanation, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I am. If there is no list, there is no list.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With the Court's indulgence and I apologise I do have some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] We still don't have the right document on the screen, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We may be able to assist. If we have the ERN, we may be able to call it up I believe on Sanction or go through another document already in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It has a number R 0082071. It's a two-page document, the next page would obviously be 72.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it -- has it been given already a Defence 2D--

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I thought it did. That's why I gave it. On my records I have it as 2D17 and that's obviously not accurate. Much to my chagrin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you could check that. Do you have your own copy that you could put on the ELMO? I know that you said there are some personal notes there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: They are not -- they are just some calculations that I made, but I can do -- yes of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I think that will speed up matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm being assured by our staff that there is nothing in the records with the number that you --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll check that. My apologies to the Court and to counsel. Thank you, Your Honour. I think it might be 2D03, because 3 was the third document. Thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: All I'd like for us to do is if we can scroll down or move the document, so we could see if it's on the ELMO to the latter portion of the document. It's on e-court now, they said? So I could have mine maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you can -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Joseph, I know your time is valuable and I'll try to short circuit this. Now, if you look at that last paragraph on that first page which is, I think, paragraph 4 directing your attention to the third sentence there starting with the letters "ABiH." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 4, third sentence, beginning ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: ABiH 2nd corps report, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: They report what, a further 4.000 DP, which is displaced persons, mostly soldiers including some civilians have entered the Tuzla area, correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. This is an UN report. Do you recognise it at all?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I didn't -- I don't recall ever seeing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know the parties who are either sending or receiving this outgoing cable? Do you recognise them, I take it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you flip back to the top, it was Akashi as I recall sending this to UN headquarters in New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, is there any reason we should doubt that, that it was reported to them at the United Nations or to some United Nations personnel that there were 4.000 Muslim men who arrived, most soldiers, some civilians, in the Tuzla area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he has already confirmed to you that he has no knowledge of that. So how can you expect him to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How is it possible, Mr. Joseph, with all due respect that you didn't notice 4.000 Muslim men on July 19th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It's asked and answered, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He simply didn't -- doesn't know about it. He never knew about it then and he doesn't know about it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who, sir, was the person in charge from the United Nations standpoint, UNPROFOR or others, to gather this type of information if it wasn't the civil affairs officer, to determine how many men, how many women may have arrived from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been -- with respect to military, you would have had mainly UNPROFOR military, but it might well have been the civil affairs officer there, Ken Biser, who was the guy, and I may well have been already deployed to Sarajevo at the time this message occurred. But I would add that I think one can state fairly that UNPROFOR was not omniscient about the situation in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What About other information, and we're talking about the Honourable Judge Prost's question, you may have had at that time. What else would have been available to the UNPROFOR or the civil affairs officer or officers, military, to obtain information of what was happening to those men from Srebrenica on July 19th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, what other sources?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of what was happening?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Presumably, if the -- up to the point that the Dutch were still there, they -- and were observing, presumably, the Dutch, but I'm not privy, I don't know when the Dutch actually pulled out so -- but presumably that would be the source. There was no civil affairs presence, there never was a civil affairs presence in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you aware, sir, that from time to time, there were some conversation that were being purportedly being intercepted between various parties? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't and I wasn't privy to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir if there were ever any aerial images that were being taken of places by various governmental agencies in or around the Srebrenica or Zepa area in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, I understood that the US had gotten -- had taken these images which apparently showed mass graves, et cetera, but I wasn't aware of that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want to discuss another topic with you, and this is the topic of screening. You mentioned it a couple times. Are you familiar, sir, with the term "triage"?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And is that the process for screening military-aged men, in essence?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Triage, I'm familiar with the term in the concept of a dealing with the -- a result of a disaster where you triage the people who can be saved, those who are beyond saving, and then those who can be saved you make some --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: A priority list?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Priority, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You never heard that term from a military standpoint, is that what you're telling me?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the context in which I've heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So you've never heard it in a military context, correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not other than the context I've conveyed to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You stated on page 45 yesterday in lines 21 through 27 that in general terms, if you have a male of military age, you were perceived to be military by the then-governing perceptions of things. Do you remember basically that comment you made?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And who had that perception, sir? All the parties?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that was -- that was just the generalised perception. If you were military age, a male of military age, was sort of -- would be perceived to be military.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If you capture a POW or an enemy combatant and you want to screen him or triage him, to set a priority to see if he has more or less information, how would you go about doing that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think this is far beyond the scope of any direct or cross-examination that's been undertaken so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you have to say to that, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I know Mr. Joseph actually is a fact witness, but he raised the issue of screening, and I'm just trying to follow if he has any other knowledge about that. And if he simply doesn't, I can move on. I just don't want any comments that he made in connection with screening to be utilised because he wasn't involved necessarily in that process if it involved prisoners of war and enemy combatants. So I could live with that if that's what Mr. Thayer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But there is agreement that he was not involved in that process, what's the point of proceeding further with your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I thank you for the agreement, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't qualify my statements. I'm just putting it to you, if there is agreement, I don't think it can be disputed that he himself was not involved in the screening process, what's the point of putting the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just because he mentioned it several times Your Honour in his two and a half days of testimony, but I'll move on if the court wishes again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir directing your attention to your involvement directly in Zepa, can you tell us sir the extent of the involvement that the Bosnian Muslim government in Sarajevo had with respect to both the surrender and evacuation of that enclave?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, especially as I see the record, it shows that they were heavily involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that the local Bosnian Muslim leadership in Zepa, when I say local, were not willing to fight on and had been trying to negotiate a surrender or an evacuation for several days but couldn't do so because of the pressure that was put to them by the Bosnian Muslims in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I honestly can't speak to that one way or the other. I'm not trying to suggest that it wasn't the case. I just simply cannot really speak to that. I don't know that I really can shed any light on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You were there. You don't remember that? You negotiated with Minister Muratovic. You don't remember that at all, Mr. Joseph?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was with Muratovic in Sarajevo prior to returning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question was asked and answered and now the questions are getting argumentative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Agreed. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Move to your next question because in any case, the witness has answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness to follow up on that question 6D29, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's a sit report memorandum dated 26th of July 1995. It's the same one we just looked at, Mr. Joseph, moments ago, with respect to Lieutenant Colonel Baxter. If I can kindly ask that the second page be shown again. Now instead of looking at the second paragraph let's read the first paragraph where Mr. Baxter is informing Mr. Harland as what his feelings were based on his assessment of the situation in Zepa, the same situation that you were involved in for several days negotiating with various parties. Do you see what Mr. Baxter feelings were at that time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assessment at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, the first paragraph on the top.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Right. That's certainly his assessment and his feeling as is reported there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, is it true, sir, that when you first started negotiating with Minister Muratovic that he actually, during your meeting with him in discussing the Zepa crisis, that he said that there should be an arrangement made to allow for a limited evacuation of those people; the Bosnians would like to withdraw? Do you remember that at all? This would have been on or about July 23rd, 1995?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: My memory of that meeting is really limited to what I see in the record, and it sounds certainly plausible to me and could be the case. I'd have to, you know, look back. I don't have a vivid recollection of that meeting, and I'm trying to work with you here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I appreciate that and I'm just going to direct your attention to 5D416 because we haven't discussed it, but it's a document that has been used previously. And as it comes up I'm just going to directs your attention to the first paragraph where it identifies yourself and Mr. Harland as being in a meeting with Minister Muratovic and then the three points that the minister asked you or asked -- yeah, you to convey to the Serbs. It's on the second page, please. If you could just scroll down a little bit for Mr. Joseph and us, and I think it's the second -- it's in the middle of the paragraph, the second point, I guess, ii, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: "There should be an arrangement made to allow for a limited evacuation of those people the Bosnians would like to withdraw?"

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who are those people that they were referencing during that meeting on or about July 23rd, 1995?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honest, genuinely I don't know, I honestly don't know. That's all I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe I'll try to refresh your recollection. Do you think Minister Muratovic was trying to evacuate certain civilians or was he more concerned in your view, since you met him, that he was trying to evacuate certain military soldiers that he had in the area?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might well have been that he was trying to evacuate civilians, it's possible and to leave the military there. It's quite possible that that was what he had on his mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But you don't remember as you sit here, correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honestly, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know that five days later on the 28th of July, 1995, the same sit report, same type of sit report, and I don't have the number but it's R0123906 is the cover page, and on that sit report, sir, it's again from David Harland to John Ryan copying various people, on July 28th 1995 is the date. The subject is "Negotiations on Zepa [11]." On that it talks about the various meetings that you may have attended, et cetera, in the second to the last paragraph, I'll read it for the sake -- I could put it on the screen. If the Court allows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On the ELMO, if you would prefer it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it would be more practical at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: My learned friend I'm just going to direct him to that last page and the Court, but if the Court would like to look at the front first pages to show that the date is actually the 28th, I'd be happy to show it, or if Mr. Joseph would like to see it he's welcome to do so?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are we looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If would you like to look at the front page to see the date?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure, sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If we can just scroll down, there we go, we're perfect there. I have it a little highlighted there, and I look at the second to the last paragraph which starts, "At about 12 noon." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You can read it to yourself and we can all read it. At that point, sir, July 28th, the civilians were evacuated, correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it seems at least at that point that with the involvement of the civil affairs office, yourself and Mr. Harland, that the minister was still holding out for a surrender. Was he not?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You really have to talk to David Harland about this. Because he was in Sarajevo all through these memoranda, and he was dealing with this. And we were getting just dribs and drabs in Zepa, and I had only that one meeting with Muratovic prior to going back. So we were there dealing with Tolimir and company and Palic, et cetera, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's fair sir, and thank you for that, and we will try to get to Mr. Harland to explain some of this for us. Now, am I correct if I wanted to summarise kind of your involvement, at least in Zepa with all due respect, that the evacuation lasted probably three days or a little over? Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know really whether it was two or three days. I don't -- we would have to refer to these memoranda to determine. It might have been two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the atmosphere was very tense during the whole time, correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The atmosphere was very stressful, very stressful. That I can tell you. And as I explained, there was spontaneous semi-riot that ensued. There were other examples of nerves being on edge and tension.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you, your team, managed to get all those people who had come to the centre and were willing to go boarding the vehicles, correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Those who came were there. We boarded, and got them out. Whether they made it to their destination or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But I'm using the word specifically, sir, "willing to go." You agree with me on that, do you not?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I tried to say, most respectfully, the question of volition to me was rather overtaken by the military situation there, and one -- you'd have to have an argument and a discussion and debate, and I'm not sure the Court would want, about the meaning of "willing" is. If someone feels that if they stay at their home, they will be killed. Is that -- and then you come in and say, "get on the buses," is that willing or is that not willing. I mean, don't know if we need to take the time to debate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think this issue was thoroughly dealt with, particularly during the cross-examination of Madam Fauveau. So I suggest that if there is anything extra or different that you would like to ask the witness, please by all means do so by all means, but otherwise don't put questions which more or less or not more or less, which the witness has already clearly given his position on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President I was just leading up to my point actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Speakers overlapping]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- on the same page, but it's actually I wanted to ask him a couple of other follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, in preparation for your testimony, if I may -- in preparation for your testimony, were you able to review your witness statement and information report?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if it's the one I think you're referring to, I had that opportunity, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: There were two reports, one a witness statement which you gave on the 11th of April 2003 to the ICTY Office of the Prosecutor, correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be correct. I don't have that in front of me but -- and I don't have a photographic memory so -- but, yes, I had an opportunity to review these statements, yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the information report was done, as you even earlier said, telephonically by an attorney, trial attorney, Salvador Viada, and an investigator, Olli Salo, on or about -- sorry, February 9th, 2005?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: One report was done telephone, another report was done in person and another -- the one -- with Olli Salo, I believe, that was the one by telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's the one we looked. Can we have 4D111 up on the screen please, again?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I can have the third page of that document? Which bears the last three ERN numbers 305 on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, your attention is being drawn by the interpreters that they are finding difficulties in catching up with both of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I do sincerely apologise. I'm trying to go slow and try to keep within the time limits given that the break is approaching but I do apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is not the first time, Mr. Ostojic. It's not the tone of your speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I understand fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I was told when I was a little boy that the way to have -- the way to heaven is covered with good intentions. So let's try to make the interpreters' life a little bit less difficult. It already is, Mr. Ostojic, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm directing your attention to the interview that you gave telephonically to the Office of the Prosecutor, specifically paragraph 17 of that interview. Do you see that, where you, sir, discuss with them how long the evacuation lasted?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do sow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Basically all I did was read that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It applies to you as well, Mr. Joseph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Joseph I'm almost done, and I apologise if I've interrupted you. I'm directing your attention to paragraph 17 of this Exhibit 4 D111. And there, apparently the investigator, the trial attorney and the investigator who interviewed you telephonically, they wrote down or recorded, as they say on the first page, what your comments were as you remembered them in 2005, and you clearly used the word "willing," correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. You can see the word "willing" on that report. And may well have used it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And no where, at least in this paragraph or this report, did you discuss the issue of duress or fear of the civilians that you were evacuating; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour with that question I would request that the witness be provided an opportunity to review the rest of the report. I think that would be only fair before he answers that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, this witness has already stated that he's reviewed the report in preparation for his testimony earlier this week and possibly before. But it's not a question of finding it. It's clearly not in that paragraph. I don't know what the objection is other than that it might be to coach the witness into not answering the question, but I find it inappropriate unless there is a legal basis to make an objection to a question. The witness is sophisticated enough, as we've seen, and intelligent enough, as we've seen, that he doesn't need Mr. Thayer to tell him that he might need the report in order to quantify or qualify his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My experience tells me that this debate should not be continued in the presence of the witness if it is to be continued in the first place. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If the witness wishes to -- have the opportunity to look at the document, then of course he's -- he is old enough and experienced enough to ask, and such -- and then we'll decide, but I don't think at this point we should discuss this any further. Mr. Joseph?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would you like me to restate the question, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Maybe I'll try to avoid so that it doesn't draw another helpful objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Joseph, do you remember whether you talked to the investigator and the trial attorney in 2005, that you told them anything about this fear and duress that you spoke about in your testimony here in open court regarding the civilians in Zepa in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sitting here today, I can't recall without looking at the whole report there what all I said about duress. I can tell you that even the very paragraph that you are referring to states that the atmosphere was very tense. If you would like me to elaborate as to the source of that tension, I'm happy to do so. It is from the fact that the Serbs had taken the pocket. That was the source of the tension, the very tension that is mentioned in this paragraph, and there may be other references elsewhere in the document there. I genuinely believe that I've addressed this trying honestly to work with you in my testimony and nothing will convince me that there was not great, great fear on the part of those departing, nothing will convince me of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't want to interrupt you much, Mr. Ostojic, but I don't know if you wish really to proceed with this line of questions, especially considering what is contained in the last sentence of the next paragraph in the same document. "However, the civilian in Zepa seem to have some information of the events in Srebrenica. And this was a factor which made them be even more concerned of their safety." Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And with all due respect to my learned friend, Your Honour, he referred specifically to the report. We can look right at this page, as Your Honour has done, and look at paragraph 13. We can just settle the issue right now, right here, while the document is in e-court and avoid wasting further time on redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know if you wish to pursue this line of questions, but I think the perspective of the use of the word "willing to go," words "willing to go" in this section, if you isolate them from the rest of the context of the same document and of his testimony, where does it get you?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm not debating with the witness. I just wanted him to clarify that those were his words that he used in his statement, and I think I'm beyond that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Whatever the Court wishes, I will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to just -- another topic just quickly and that's on the involvement of the Bosnian military in the attack that they may have had on the UNPROFOR units in Zepa. Were you familiar before your assignment the extent of their threats or actual attack on those various observation posts or buildings?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I believe I testified, we were aware that there were these allegations. I may have even been aware of some of the reports about this. I don't know that I had confirmation of any of this. And I don't recall, and I'm stressing recollection here, I don't recall that aspect being impressed upon me by the Ukrainians when we arrived. I concede that events that I was not witness to might have transpired. I simply can't testify to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about only the events that and the facts that you know, so you didn't know that the UNPROFOR observation posts were overrun on July 19th, 1995, for example?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Overrun by whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The Bosnian government forces.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you know, sir, that the UNPROFOR observation posts were disarmed, a number of them, in fact, by the Bosnian government forces?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I've tried to testify, what we observed with my own eyes, which is most -- hopefully most relevant to this Court, these proceedings, is that I saw when I came, I believe it was the 20th, that the Observation Post 2 had been overrun by the Serb army. That's the part that I can testify to. I simply can't testify to the other part, and this witness is not stating that it did or didn't happen. This witness simply can't testify to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me show you this exhibit again with the Court's assistance because it doesn't have an exhibit number, but it's a situation report dated the 19th of July 1995, and I promise you it's the last exhibit, and with ERN or bait stamp number R 0123425, it's a memorandum from Mr. David Harland to John Ryan with I believe Mr. Edward Joseph's name, I believe right under Mr. Harland's. Sir I'm directing your attention while you're looking at that to the very last paragraph of that first page where I was actually reading from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What page?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, page 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. I think I stated that we were aware of these threats and allegations, and I believe I stated yesterday that or the day before, I've lost track now, of -- that Silajdzic had denied it and I make no judgement as to Silajdzic veracity or whether or not he was telling the truth. I make no judgement whatsoever. So I don't know what more -- how I can say to you about this. Yes, we were aware of these allegations. Whether in fact what happened, whether these observation posts were in fact overrun, whether there had been heavy machine-gun fire that had been mentioned in another, I don't -- I was not witness to any of that. I don't recall the Ukrainians talking to us about any of that. I also don't recall any hostility showed by the Ukrainians towards Palic in the entire time that I was there and that he was in the compound and had he been directing heavy machine-gun fire at them, and had one might have expected that. I'm -- that is something I can tell you I didn't observe and I was in a position to observe that, and I observed no apparent hostility manifested towards Palic from the Ukrainians. Whether that's conclusive or not, I don't know. I can only tell you what I observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Mr. Joseph, I'm not asking you about the incidents which you just described which was after your return to Zepa during the negotiations of both the surrender and the evacuation. I'm asking you on the first day that you got there, on the 19th of July 1995, or the 20th, as you sometimes thought that it was, on those early days, we are not talking about Silajdzic now and those negotiations where threats were allegedly made. We are talking about your document from -- with your name on it, with the senior civil affairs officer's name on it, describing exactly what happened. Nowhere in that third paragraph does it, sir, say, "someone has alleged that they've overrun the observation posts." Do they?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I've lost the thread of your question. I'm sorry, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You're mixing the issues that we've discussed yesterday and today with you with respect to Silajdzic. This has nothing no do with the threat that may or may not have been made on or about July 23 or 25, 1995. This is actually a report, your initial report, setting forth precisely that which you and your senior civil affairs officers understood the situation to be in Zepa on the 19th of July 1995. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I think I've already stated so, that, yes, this reflects that we understood there were these threats, yes, correct. Their full extent, I can't attest to simply because I'm not in -- I thought that was the reason for this further questioning. I'm sorry, I thought you were trying to get me to provide, shed some more light or something on this. That would --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd like you to shed more light, but how many observation posts did the Bosnian government forces overrun? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that they overran any or all. I don't know. I'll say that again. I don't know that they overran any or that they overran all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you don't know how many they disarmed, if any, correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that they disarmed any or that they disarmed all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And who would know that? Mr. Harland, do you think?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harland might know that. Someone in the military chain would better know that, and I would best direct you, if I can say so respectfully, if you're having General Smith, I can think of no better source than General Smith, or perhaps one of the Ukrainian officers who were present on the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And one final question, sir. Where would the civil affairs officers obtain such information? Would that have been from General Smith?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have -- waiting. It could have been anywhere in the military chain. It didn't necessarily have to be General Smith. It could have been from some operations officer, it could have been anywhere in the chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Joseph. It was my pleasure.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Mr. Zivanovic, but I think it's time for the break. You still require 20 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we'll have a 25-minute break now, and I think you need to regulate yourselves. We'll have 20 minutes for sure after the break, plus if there is going to be re-examination, you would know how long that's going to take. I still have to inquire whether we have questions from here but I doubt it. So make your own assessment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to advise the Court that Mr. McCloskey had to attend to an urgent case-related matter. If he resolves it, he will rejoin us but he had to tear himself away from the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And will you be raising the issue that we were informed that you would like to raise a matter, and we told you let's leave it until after -- you will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Two very brief matters, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Joseph.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to focus all of my questions on the time that you spent at the air base in Tuzla. This was sometime in mid-July 1995. The day before yesterday, on direct, you mentioned a female who was clutching on to the barbed wire fence, and you also told us that you had spoken to her. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: She told you that she was expecting the arrival of men from Srebrenica, that she had heard that they were around there, and that she was hoping to maybe find her husband or her son among them?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: She had heard a rumour that the men were encamped there on adjacent -- on an adjacent part of the Tuzla air base, which was not true of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that at the time the men from Srebrenica had not arrived there at all?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the air base. That is for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me whether you asked her if she was so eager to see that, why she didn't leave through a gate, why she didn't leave by a normal way to check whether the relatives that she was looking for had indeed arrived?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 1, we were aware of no men. I certainly was not aware of any men who had arrived there, number 1. So I was not aware to suggest any other access point for her to theoretically be relocated with her loved ones, so that's -- that's why I would not have had any useful suggestion for her -- for her.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not mean that you were to give her any suggestions as to what to do, but why didn't you ask her why she was climbing on to the wire -- barbed wire fence, why she didn't opt to leave through the gate?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: She had heard -- as far as I can remember, she was at one point in the camp where she had heard the men are just on this other side, and there was no gate at that point. There was this barbed wire fence, as far as I can recall, and she was standing there attempting tentatively to try to scale and then step back and scale, and to do her best to try to get over it when I approached her and then that conversation took place, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether, in front of the base, at the time, there were any displaced persons hanging around, not in the base, within the perimeter, but outside the perimeter of the base?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that. We were flooded with displaced persons. I think this memorandum, the -- one of them, I think the one from Akashi used the figure of 25.000. So we had 25.000 displaced persons coming to this location within two days. Is it possible that some of them were placed outside the gate? I suppose it's possible. And I know we were overwhelmed, so indeed it's quite possible that some were outside the gate. I don't recall any male displaced persons at that time. I only recall female displaced persons, aside from perhaps some children.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you an exhibit, which is 1D373. Could you please look at the document, because I am going to put some questions to you based on that document. Kindly look at the document, the date is 14th July 1995. Could you please look at the item 1(D) of this document?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm looking at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me whether it is indicated here that on that date, in front of the base, there were 9.000 people, some of whom tried to break into the base but the base could not accommodate them. And if they entered the base on their own, they might stray across minefields on the base?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me to confirm that this is what this documents says?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can all read it. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I am asking you whether this might have been the reason for which this woman could not leave the base via a gate, but, rather, opted to climb over the fence.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can tell you is how I remember the events, sir. All I can tell you is how I remember the event. Whether there was a connection -- I'm in fact glad that you put this here because it shows just how bad I used the term overwhelmed and that's reflected here in the document, and that's where our attentions were, and I'm telling you this is how I remember this event. I remember it distinctly, and whether it was because these people were grouped outside or for some other reason she for some reason had heard that the men were there, that's how I recall the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During your tour of duty in Tuzla, which lasted for about a week, did you learn about the arrival of the men from Srebrenica? Did you receive any such information?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I tell you I really don't recall hearing about that. Is it possible that there was some mention of some -- I -- my best recollection is I -- I don't remember. I remember that being a question mark. I remember that being a question mark. If that doesn't accord with what actually happened, I can't say, I'm only giving you my recollection that that was the fate of the men was a question mark. That was as I recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you collect any data about that from others?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the fate of the men or?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: About the people arriving from Srebrenica, how many arrived from Srebrenica, whether they indeed arrived, when if they did, had anybody been killed on the way there, what their fate was, or similar information?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have been natural, very natural, for UNPROFOR and the UNHCR, to collect all of that data, and it's possible I was even privy to some of it. I'm telling you here, August, 2007, I don't recall terribly much about that, and there -- perhaps we were made aware of maybe some who had arrived or something like that but in my -- my general recollection is that the fate of the men, at least the vast majority, was a giant question mark. That's my recollection today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you also tell me, please, whether displaced persons who arrived in Tuzla, were ever registered? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have been the role of UNHCR. That would have been exactly their mandate. And that was not our mandate but that was their role, and I presumably these people were registered. I would presume that they would do that. We were -- we were there at the air base dealing with this situation that Akashi is saying is bad and rapidly growing worse. That was our primary focus, and working with everyone, throwing ourselves into it, to try to best address that immediate situation. That was our -- that was our focus.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you come by the information that a certain number of people who were not accommodated at the air base were accommodated at the so-called collection centres? Did you come by that information? And did you ever learn the number of the people who might have been accommodated in that way?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I recall now. I don't remember that. It's possible -- let's -- it's possible that UNHCR was taking some of the people to collective centres. We were dealing with this displaced persons influx crisis at the air base, so I was not aware of this other information. I'm sure UNHCR has good records on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look at another report. This is 1D374. The date is July the 17th, as you may well see. If I'm not mistaken, your name can be found here as the drafter of the document. Could you please explain whether this means that you were the one who drafted or prepared this report?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As they say it in French, "bien joue." [In English] Yes, indeed it appears that I was the drafter of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please try and tell us whether on that same page, under the title, "Main points," if you look at the first sentence, the first bullet point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If -- Mr. Joseph, if you could put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have a second copy to put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's very strange. Your number is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My number is correct but it is not in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any way, let's speed this up. It's on the ELMO now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The first sentence reads, "Men who fled Srebrenica arrive in Tuzla area after week-long ordeal." This is the information that you had at the time. Can you now turn to page 2 of the same report? Does it say here that interviews were carried out with a certain number of persons who had all described the events that they had been through in a similar way, and does it say in the report that some 12.000 to 15.000 of them left Srebrenica between the 10th and 11th of July, that some 5.000 or 6.000 of them crossed over to the territory under the control of the 2nd Corps south of Sapna, and that this happened the night before, and that some 3.000 or up to 3.000 people had been killed on the road mostly by land mines and in fighting the Republika Srpska army troops, that an unknown number were captured, that some committed suicide, and that an unknown number of them left for Zepa? Is this the information that you were privy to at the time, the information that you had been given?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I drafted that, yes, I would have been privy to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And one more thing. Could you please look at the following page? The subtitle reads, "Collective centres." It says here that there are approximately 17.000 persons housed in collective centres, among eight different communities in the Tuzla-Drina canton. The exact number of people are given as a breakdown of these collective centres. Can you tell me whether this is the information that you had at the time, that you had been given by the authorised personnel who made the lists of those displaced persons?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Presumably, yes. It doesn't say the source, but I'm sure we had a qualified source and that's why I put it in the memo that apparently I drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is all. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Is there re-examination, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There is, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. How long will it take?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I will do my very best. I understand the path to heaven is paved with good intentions, but I will do my very best to complete the redirect in time today. I have cut my examination in half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to see Mr. Joseph stay here the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Nor would I, Mr. President. With Madam Usher's assistance, if we could just put up one document very quickly. And in fact we will have to put up a couple of documents so -- this is -- we've seen this page already. It is the third page of the witness's information report from 2005. 4D111.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You were asked where in paragraph 17 of this report did you discuss the issues of duress or fear of the civilians that you were evacuating. I just want to give you an opportunity to look at that page of the report. I turn your attention first to paragraph 11. "Next morning I saw big number of local women, children and some very old men sitting and waiting in the town square. This is a vivid memory for me, as I remember these people being very much afraid and tense, it very much reminded me of the situations with the evacuees from Srebrenica," is that accurate, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Paragraph 13, "I knew we could not happy any parties with their ethnic cleansing and therefore I approached the civilians and asked if they wanted to leave Zepa. Several of them replied that they would like to stay where their homes are and but there was no one to protect them and therefore they feel their lives being threatened. I could sense the atmosphere being very nervous, especially when they saw a VRS jeep parking nearby and some VRS soldiers stepping out, the clear message these civilians gave to was that they were terrified if they were left alone with the VRS;" is that correct, sir? Is that what you told the investigators over the phone?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, particularly the last part I think some licence might have been taken with the English and the phrasing, especially in the first sentence there, but that -- the gist is absolutely correct, and I think I've so testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I want to turn your attention to the draft militarisation agreement, and again I'm afraid we are going to need -- it will I think just be faster if we put it up on the ELMO. Just page 1. You've been shown this by several of my friends. I just note that if you turn your attention to the first two paragraphs, the -- where it says, "if you can see it, Bosnian Serb forces continue to bombard the safe area of Zepa and its civilian population with heavy weapons and continue to make armed incursions into the safe area." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Second paragraph, "Bosnian Serb forces have also subjected UNPROFOR troops to attacks with small arms and heavy weapons. They have further threatened to intensify these attacks, especially against the peacekeepers in an observation post which is surrounded by Serb mines if NATO launches air attacks." Now, you are the author of this draft agreement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Co-author, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall the source or sources of this information?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been the same with respect to allegations about what the army was doing. It would have been from UNPROFOR military, probably, that's where we would have gotten the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sit-reps or civ-reps?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In conversations with operations officers and UNPROFOR military.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to show you another document. And for the record, it is 03279250 through 9252. This has been previously disclosed to the Defence. If we could Madam Usher just turn to the second page first? This is a memo dated 15 July, it's a Sector Sarajevo weekly situation report. The heading is, "Serb assault on Zepa begins, UNPROFOR forces under attack by the Serbs are powerless." You see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see the second paragraph where it says "the Ukrainians remained in position and shortly after 1500 the Serbs began to bombard them and the Bosnian forces around the perimeter of the enclave?"

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could turn to the next page, do you see the top where it says, UNPROFOR's position in the pocket has also been difficult. The 79 Ukrainians in the pocket have been under Serb bombardment since 27 June with the tempo increasing this week? Early in the week, the Serbs tried to force the Ukrainians out of OP 9 at the southern end of the pocket. Later in the week OPs 1, 2 and 3 at the south western end of the pocket were also attacked. You see that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the next paragraph, "The attacks came after an ultimatum from the Serbs delivered on 30 June that UNPROFOR should withdraw from the pocket immediately."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but before you answer that question, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I know that the Prosecutor is in a hurry, but I really do not see the point of reading out this document. Could the witness say whether he remembers anything of the events of the last days in Zepa? I -- the date of 27 June has been mentioned here and the 15th of July too.
